newsitem.title: KENYA: Rebel advance sends Zaire troops fleeing.
newsitem.headline: Rebel advance sends Zaire troops fleeing.

text.p: Routed Zairean army troops, reportedly looting and raping as they go, fled through eastern Zaire on Monday as advancing rebels moved north after capturing another key town.

Missionaries reported the Rwanda-backed rebels took the town of Beni after heavy fighting on Saturday and were now moving further north towards the larger town of Bunia, reported to be in complete chaos.
"Beni fell on Saturday. Rebels moved swiftly to capture Beni after taking the town of Butembo," one of the sources told Reuters, quoting missionaries evacuated from eastern Zaire.

A report from Action by Churches Together (ACT), a Geneva-based umbrella grouping of missionary organisations, said several soldiers had fled towards Bunia from which most international staff now had been evacuated.

"The soldiers are reported to loot as they flee. Reports of significant numbers of rapes by the soldiers are coming from the area. Some women are reported to have died from very violent rapes and rape attempts," Information Officier Nils Carstensen stated in the report.

A plane flying over the area on Monday said 47 Zairean army vehicles were heading along the road north from Beni towards Mambasa where it was expected they would turn westwards to the regional capital of Kisangani, also reported to be in turmoil.
Another missionary group, based in Nairobi, told Reuters they were still in contact with local aid workers in Bunia.

"The rebel focus is now on Bunia where we are told Zairean soldiers are fleeing in total panic. The rebels are advancing along the road to Bunia, there is complete chaos in Bunia," said one radio operator.

Mission Aviation Fellowship (MAF), which provides logistical support for missionaries in the field, said it was evacuating its main base at Niakunde, about 24 kms (15 miles) west of Bunia, due to the instability in the region.
"We are hoping to bring our last people out on Monday evening, we fear Zairean troops will sack the place as they pass through," said one MAF official.
Eight Egyptian military advisers flew out of Bunia on Monday, missionary sources said.
The Egyptians managed to board what could be the last missionary flight for some time out of Bunia and landed at Entebbe in neighbouring Uganda, the sources said.
It was not clear how long the Egyptians had been in Zaire or what exactly their mission was.
Beni, so far the northernmost town to fall to the rebels, is close to where the Ugandan army has been attacking Ugandan rebels based on the Zairean side of the border.
Shortly before the town fell, businessmen in radio contact with missionary organisations in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi reported Ugandan soldiers were involved in the fighting.
"It was not clear at first if the town had fallen to the rebels or the Ugandans," said one radio operator. He added there had been a total radio silence since its fall.
Zaire has accused Uganda of attacking and occupying the town of Kasindi, 60 km (35 miles) southeast of Beni and 10 km (six miles) inside Zaire.
Uganda says it shelled Kasindi to neutralise Ugandan rebels in the area but denies crossing the border.
Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni has close ties with the Rwandan military strongman, Vice-President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame and Rwanda openly supports the Tutsi-led Zairean rebels.
Kagame's Tutsi rebels drove Hutu government forces out of Rwanda in 1994 after the slaughter of an estimated one million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The Zairean rebels, who call themselves the Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), now control much of eastern Zaire, including the towns of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma and Butembo.
The ADFL rebels have vowed to take their military campaign in Africa's second largest country to the capital Kinshasa.

Regional experts believe the rebel strategy is to take Bunia, confirming their hold on a large swathe of eastern Zaire along the borders of Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda, and then turn westwards towards Kisangani and Kindu.
Africa's latest conflict was ignited by Zaire's attempts to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group that first came to Zaire from Rwanda nearly 200 years ago.
